flashcards.q: Why does CPython need the GIL, mechanistically?
flashcards.a: Reference counting is a read-modify-write race without synchronization -- two threads incrementing/decrementing the same object's count concurrently can corrupt it, causing a premature free (use-after-free) or a leak. The GIL prevents this by ensuring only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time.

flashcards.q: Why does threading help I/O-bound Python code despite the GIL, but not CPU-bound code?
flashcards.a: CPython explicitly releases the GIL around blocking I/O calls, letting other threads run Python bytecode while one waits on the OS -- genuine concurrency. CPU-bound code never blocks on I/O, so the GIL just round-robins between threads with zero parallelism gain.

flashcards.q: What is biased reference counting and why did it succeed where the Gilectomy project failed?
flashcards.a: It keeps a cheap non-atomic ref count for the common case (single-thread-owned objects), falling back to atomic/shared counting only when an object is actually accessed cross-thread. Gilectomy applied atomic ops/locks uniformly to every ref count update, devastating single-threaded performance with no correspondingly compelling speedup.

flashcards.q: Free-threaded Python status as of 3.14 -- default or opt-in? Overhead?
flashcards.a: Officially supported (no longer experimental) starting 3.14, but opt-in (python3.14t build), not the default python3.14. Roughly 5-10% single-threaded overhead vs the GIL build. GIL-disabled-by-default is projected for 2028-2030.

flashcards.q: Why does swapping ThreadPoolExecutor for CPU-bound work never raise an error even though it's wrong?
flashcards.a: Both Thread/ProcessPoolExecutor share an identical interface and both return correct results -- ThreadPoolExecutor on CPU-bound work just fails to parallelize (GIL still serializes), producing no speedup with no exception. Only a benchmark of actual scaling catches this; a correctness test suite passes either way.

flashcards.q: Why does multiprocessing sidestep the GIL entirely, and what's its main cost?
flashcards.a: Separate OS processes each have their own interpreter, GIL, and memory space -- no shared reference-counting race to solve. Cost: data crossing process boundaries must be pickled/unpickled, which dominates for frequent small payloads.

flashcards.q: Does the periodic GIL 'switch interval' provide any CPU-bound parallelism speedup?
flashcards.a: No -- it only forces fairness (threads take turns holding the GIL), preventing starvation. It doesn't change the one-thread-at-a-time execution constraint; threads still run strictly sequentially, just with more frequent handoffs, potentially adding overhead without adding speedup.

flashcards.q: What does multiprocessing.shared_memory solve, and what does it NOT provide?
flashcards.a: Solves redundant per-worker copying of large read-heavy data (default pickling would copy it into every worker's own memory). Does NOT provide synchronization for concurrent writes -- still needs an explicit Lock for that.

flashcards.q: Will free-threaded Python eventually eliminate the need for multiprocessing?
flashcards.a: No -- free-threading solves single-process, single-machine CPU parallelism only. It provides no fault isolation (a crash in one thread can take down the whole process, unlike separate processes) and no multi-machine scaling, both of which remain reasons to use multiprocessing/distributed processes.
